item.title: Why We’re All In Love With Erling Haaland
item.description:
Relationships

Why We’re All In Love With Erling Haaland

A look at the science behind an emerging World Cup mass obsession.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Strength combined with the ability to protect amplifies a man's attractiveness.
  • Erling Haaland exhibits this in addition to perceived kindness, loyalty, and humor.
  • These qualities may be interacting to amplify his appeal, helping to explain an international obsession.

Spend more than five seconds on social media and you’ll come across a plethora of posts, memes, and even songs about Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland. The 6’5” striker with shoulder length blonde hair has been garnering the attention of World Cup enthusiasts and non-sports fans alike for his goal-scoring prowess, humorous Snapchat uploads, and even his love of designer bags. Very few people have strong criticisms to lob against him, and when they do it’s mostly related to the technicality of his game, not necessarily his personality or behavior.

Haaland has also struck a particular chord with women, whose fanfare for and attraction towards the alleged Golden Retriever in a Viking Body has placed among the top 10 “Sexiest Sportsmen on the Planet.”

Why are we so drawn to Erling Haaland? Let’s take a look at some of the more science-backed reasons.

1. Ability to Protect

Sure, a man’s physical strength is inherently attractive. But strength alone doesn’t always cut it, especially if that strength is used to intimidate or control in a coercive manner. Much more alluring is when a man’s strength is used to protect others, as a 2025 study by Barlev et al. found. Haaland repeatedly positions himself between teammates and defenders during penalty and corner kicks. Multiple clips from live games show him helping teammates and even opponents off the ground, checking in on players after potential injuries, and going in for hugs with rivals after heated matches. This may signal Haaland’s ability not just to be strong and exert brute force when charging down the field or scoring a goal from an upside down kick, but also that he can and does use his strength wisely.

2. Perceived Self-Control Under Pressure

While most of us have not spent any time with Haaland IRL, his public behavior appears to indicate that he has strong emotional control—at least, most of the time. This is evidenced by his ability to not react even when exceedingly provoked by opponents. Haaland is known for rarely retaliating (except, perhaps, when opponents mess with his hair) despite getting grabbed, wrestled, pulled on, and collided into by multiple opponents. Emotional control—and self-control in general—has consistently been shown to be a highly desirable trait in male partners, especially when considering them as long-term mates. This could also help explain Haaland's allure.

3. Ostensible Kindness

Haaland has been seen multiple times and has developed a reputation for his kindness to his fans. Seeing so many examples of Haaland's generosity with his followers may be making a lot of us swoon. Multiple studies have demonstrated that prosocial behavior such as kindness enhances how attractive and beautiful people are rated to be. This is true for both men and women, by the way. Prosociality (a broader scientific term encompassing kindness, warmth, generosity, compassion, and other beneficial-to-others qualities) can even outrank intelligence in beauty evaluations, enhancing someone’s physical appeal above and beyond looks and smarts alone.

4. Apparent Loyalty

One of the most desirable traits in a long-term mate, loyalty is a highly attractive quality in male and female partners alike. Perhaps all of us are perceiving Haaland’s loyalty by the way he appears to prioritize and care for his long-term partner Isabel Haugseng Johnasen, with whom he has a son. Think the time he ensured—despite being awash in the final celebration for Manchester City’s UEFA Champions League—that she had an actual chair to sit on so she didn’t have to pop a squat on the ground.

Naysayers might argue that loyalty isn't the most accurate term for Haaland's behavior, given that he hasn’t proposed to his partner of many years. But it’s important to note that Norway doesn’t have a strong marriage culture. Marriage isn’t as economically advantageous in Norway as it is in some other countries and marriage is largely considered a later symbolic step in a very long-term relationship than a relationship’s real beginning. So give the guy a break, alright?

5. Humor

A huge contributor to Haaland’s virality and appeal is his humor. The playfulness he injects both on and off the field (and particularly online) packs a major punch in terms of his appeal. Just scroll through his Snapchat for some examples of this. It’s likely not surprising to hear how research backs the connection between someone’s ability to make us laugh and how attractive we find them. But it’s worth noting why: Some studies suggest humor signals someone is creative when it comes to problem-solving (an indicator of someone’s ability to benefit and aid us, and therefore help us survive). Others find that humor indicates a mate’s value, possibly by signaling higher intelligence. Either way, Haaland makes us laugh and that strongly adds to how favorably we view him.

The Takeaway

Haaland’s athletic ability and physical appearance aren’t the sole reasons the world is currently obsessed with him. Of course, we can’t say for sure what the Norway national team star is like out of the public eye. But in addition to his power on the field, and his looks, his widespread appeal may have a lot to do with what we all perceive as his ability to protect, his emotion regulation and self-control under pressure, his kindness and loyalty, as well as his ability to make us laugh.

item.title: Healing in Public: When Heartbreak Has an Audience
item.description:
Parasocial Relationships

Healing in Public: When Heartbreak Has an Audience

Why watching a stranger's public breakup taught me something about healing.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • A parasocial audience can soothe emotion but isn't reciprocal support.
  • Writing for an audience who shares your pain can speed genuine growth.
  • Expecting comments changes what people are willing to say honestly.
  • Public healing works best as one part of a larger support system.
Some nights, watching someone else's story feels like company.
Source: Tony Lam Hoang / Unsplash

Why I Kept Coming Back

I've been watching one creator's videos for years now. Not consistently. Some months, yes. Some topics, yes, others no. The kind of following that ebbs and flows depending on what's going on in my own life.

What pulled me back in most recently wasn't a new format or a trending sound. It was grief. She started talking openly about her mental health after a bad breakup, to an audience she can't see and mostly doesn't know by name.

Why does this pull me in more than anything else she's posted?

The Science Says Belief Matters More Than Audience Size

Journaling about pain has always helped people process it. That part isn't new. What's new is the audience.

A 2020 study in the Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media had people write about recent breakups believing an online audience would read it (Kornfield & Toma, 2020). Some were told their readers had been through something similar. Others were told the audience was general.

The people who believed their readers understood them wrote with more depth. Weeks later, they also reported more post-traumatic growth: the psychological term for actually growing from something painful, not just surviving it.

Here's the part that surprised me: This effect showed up before anyone had said a single supportive word back. Just believing you're understood seems to change how you make sense of your own story.

But There's a Catch

The same study found that people who expected comments actually wrote less about their emotions than people who didn't. Knowing you'll be watched changes what you're willing to say out loud.

I don't think that makes it dishonest, exactly. I think it means an audience edits the story a little, whether we mean it to or not. What she shares is probably not her rawest version. It's her rawest shareable version.

Why the Connection Feels Real

Part of what's kept me watching for years is something researchers first named in 1956: the parasocial relationship, or a one-directional bond with someone who doesn't know you exist (Horton & Wohl, 1956). The term is old. The research behind it isn't.

A 2020 meta-analysis pulling together 120 studies found that parasocial relationships aren't a sign that someone's real-life connections are lacking (Tukachinsky et al., 2020). They correlate with the same things that build real friendships, like feeling similar to the other person. Watching her doesn't mean I'm missing something offline. It means my brain is running the same bonding process it runs for people I actually know.

A more recent review, covering 281 studies published between 2016 and 2020, found the field has shifted almost entirely from television and film to social media (Schramm et al., 2024). It also found a growing number of studies looking specifically at what happens when a parasocial relationship ends: the quiet grief of a favorite creator going silent, deleting their account, or simply changing. That detail stopped me. I hadn't thought about what it would mean if she stopped posting.

It isn't hollow, exactly. It just isn't mutual. And it can be genuinely stabilizing in a hard moment — a sense of being less alone with a feeling, without the risk that comes with real, reciprocal closeness.

It can also become the whole plan instead of one part of it. That's the version worth watching for, in yourself or in someone you love.

What I'm Taking From This

I don't have a tidy prescription here. I'm still working out what to do with my own habit of checking in on someone else's healing. But a few things seem worth holding onto:

  1. Notice who you're picturing, not just how many people are watching. The audience-belief effect wasn't about follower count. It was about whether readers felt like people who'd get it.
  2. Watch for the gap between the post and the feeling. If a caption reads more "healed" than the person likely feels, treat that gap as information, not a failure.
  3. Keep one channel of support that isn't watching. A friend, a therapist, a page nobody else will read. Parasocial connection can regulate a feeling. It can't ask a follow-up question.

Heartbreak has always eventually needed witnesses. What's changed is how many, and how visible.

item.title: Maternal Ambivalence: A Peculiar Kind of Ambivalence
item.description:
Parenting

Maternal Ambivalence: A Peculiar Kind of Ambivalence

The reparative nature of ambivalence needs a place in the maternal literature.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Maternal ambivalence is distinct, rooted in an immutable, primal mother-child bond.
  • Ambivalence is often misunderstood as negative, but it connects rather than splits relationships.
  • Ambivalence in mothers can be reparative, transforming challenging moments into deeper love.

The psychological understanding of ambivalence needs a reset. I define it as the coexistence of contradictory feelings toward someone that occur in relationships and interactions. For too long, ambivalence has been misapprehended and saturated in negativity, becoming an untapped dynamic with the potential to offer so much. The maternal space is calling for this: an opportunity for transformation and repair, a way to improve our perception and understanding of the troubling and loving moments of mothering.

Claiming the term ambivalence

In contemporary language, the saying “two or more truths can exist at one time” is gaining traction. When I first heard this expression in everyday conversation, I felt heartened. Finally, people are beginning to grasp my understanding of ambivalence, even though the word has yet to be attached to this meaning. Hopefully, our language is carving a space for the inclusive and rather than the limiting binary or: despair and hope, happiness and sorrow, delight and disappointment.

Despite this forward movement, the word ambivalence is still mired in misapprehension. It is widely misunderstood as a negative energy and often interchanged with indifference, which is a splitting mechanism, the polar opposite of the connecting force of ambivalence. It is also diminished when described as mixed emotions or uncertainty.

While I have long maintained that the mother’s experience is a particular type of ambivalence, initially I blurred the lines between maternal ambivalence and ambivalence. As my work developed, the singular nature of maternal ambivalence has increasingly intrigued me. I am intensely curious as to why the mother’s ambivalence is so distinct. What is it in mother-child dynamics that allows the difficulties between them to be reparative for the mother?

My view is that this dyad holds a peculiar ambivalence. The mother has a unique duty of care to her child, who she is forever tied to psychically. Despite incidences of loss, death, and distancing, that child is part of the mother on a primal level. It is an immutable and enduring emotional bond that belongs with the mother. This is part of her DNA, and she carries it through her most difficult and most loving moments. Jacqueline Rose puts it so well, “there is nobody in the world I love as much as my child, nobody in the world who makes me as angry.”1

I do not consider that these feelings exist in the same way in non-maternal relationships. While both are marked by connection and conflict, the non-maternal feelings are usually clearer and less loaded. They can be accepted and worked through more objectively and perhaps more easily resolved. Mothers generally, but not always, have undergone pregnancy, birth, and child-rearing, which hold significant physical and emotional complexity. The child is born with its own story, which the mother steps into. These are often colored by deep-seated maternal triggers that are distinctive to the mother-child dynamic and background. Strong social and personal expectations, including that of an unachievable 24/7 presence and unconditional love, drive much of how the mother sees herself and how she is socially perceived.

Maternal ambivalence in the real world

The mother’s capacity to lean into all her feelings about her mothering, to accept rather than neglect the troubling ones, and to sit with her conflicting and sometimes shocking emotions can be frightening and unsettling. At the same time, these dark feelings are the key to developing an understanding of herself and her child. The unique mother-child bond adds an extra layer to the dynamic of ambivalence, and while her feelings erupt in the troubling moments of mothering, ironically, these are also healing.

Here are some illustrations of what I mean by maternal ambivalence:

  • It's 2 a.m. The new mother has been carrying her baby for three hours and is exhausted. Every time she tried to put her infant down, the screaming started again. She is full of doubts and ruminates about the last two days. Am I spoiling him? Is there something really wrong? He hasn't pooed for 24 hours. His tiny body is rigid, and she knows he is in spasms of pain. She is frayed, worried, and fed up. Suddenly, something changes. She feels her baby’s body relaxing, and the screaming stops. Her baby poops.
  • Mum has been asking her 14-year-old daughter to come to dinner. The girl is still on the computer and is ignoring her mother, who is getting increasingly annoyed and is ready to ban all devices. The mother barges angrily into her daughter’s room and finds the girl with tears streaming down her face, “All my friends are at a sleepover and I’m not invited”.
  • Its 5 a.m. and her 21-year-old son hasn't come home yet. His phone is off. She is frantic and furious. Do I call the police? I’ll start with his friends. On the fifth try, his friend answers, “He’s fallen asleep on the couch, we had a few too many drinks, we are safe.”

All these stories share commonalities. The collision of many troubling feelings, including anger, resentment, irritation, and disappointment, accompanied by guilt, pity, relief, and shame, and overwhelming sensations of love. Something melts inside the mother as moments of turbulence pierce and heal her. Her love is strengthened and transformed. This is a particular nuance in the mother-child relationship.

For the moment, all is OK in the world. The mother is renewed and ready to show up again tomorrow.

This is maternal ambivalence.

Every mother knows this on some level. This is not meant to be fixed, just lived through and understood. These are the ordinary moments of daily mothering.

item.title: Grieving Someone Still Alive: Moving On Without Closure
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Grieving Someone Still Alive: Moving On Without Closure

Family estrangement is a real loss, and still feeling it isn't a failure.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Estrangement is a form of ambiguous loss, a grief with no clear ending or timeline.
  • The pressure to "just move on" adds a layer of shame about still grieving, on top of the original loss.
  • Healing doesn't mean the grief disappears. It means carrying it without letting it run your life.
When someone is still just a phone call away, the grief rarely feels finished.
Source: Jess Yuwono / Unsplash

Whether you chose to go no contact or it was chosen for you, I think you'll know this feeling.

It’s an ordinary day, and you’re doing well. You see a Father's Day promotion in your inbox. Or a sibling's photo appears in your feed. Maybe you see a mother and daughter laughing together in the easy way you never had.

Then, out of nowhere, a pang of grief arrives. Along with a familiar question: Why does this bother me so much?

I want to say something clearly, because almost no one says it to estranged people: It’s okay to still feel sad. The problem isn't that you lack resilience, or forgiveness, or willpower. The problem is that the advice you keep being given—to just move on—misunderstands what this type of loss actually is.

I've specialized in family estrangement for over a decade. It was the focus of my doctoral research, and it's something I've lived myself. So when I talk about being told to move on, this isn't just theory for me; it's personal. I know what it's like to hear “just let it go” and feel something inside answer: I would if I could, but I don't know how.

Think about how differently we treat other losses. If a widow were told to stop dwelling on her husband’s recent death, most of us would recognize the cruelty right away. Yet people living with estrangement hear messages like that all the time — “Life's too short to hold grudges.” “Just let it go; they're family.” “Why are you still upset? It was years ago.” — and they're expected to nod along. It’s not that one loss is “bigger” than the other. It's that one kind comes with a script, and the other doesn't.

The Loss No One Prepares You For

Recovering from estrangement involves a concept called ambiguous loss, a term coined by researcher Pauline Boss. This type of loss has no solution and, therefore, no closure. You do not have the person in your life, but they are still alive. They are out there somewhere living life, posting things on social media, being talked about in groups you are not invited to, and are possibly reachable, or maybe not.

Closure is only possible with certainty and a definitive end. Neither is available with ambiguous loss.

When someone dies, the world hands you a framework. There are rituals: a funeral, cards and flowers, time off work, and space to grieve. And people typically know what to say to offer comfort. Estrangement comes with none of that. You bear a loss that's every bit as heavy, sometimes heavier, and you carry it almost completely alone.

For many people, knowing there is a name for what they are feeling is a relief. The pain doesn’t go away, but things start to make sense, and that’s when the healing work can begin.

Why the Grief Keeps Coming Back

Ordinary grief, however brutal, tends to move in one direction. Ambiguous loss circles back on you.

The loss that comes with estrangement isn't a single wound that heals with time. Instead, it reopens again and again. A birthday passes. You find out the person has rewritten the history of what happened or has been telling relatives a version of the story you barely recognize. You realize you’ve been left off an invitation because other people chose sides.

Each is a fresh encounter with the same loss, along with the unpleasant memories that go with it.

And then there's the second burden, the one that does the most damage. When other people, or your own inner voice, insist you should be over this by now, you end up carrying two things at once: the grief itself and shame about still grieving.

Now you're not just hurting; you're criticizing yourself for not being over it yet. That double weight is exhausting.

I still feel it. Mother's Day and holidays are challenging for me. I don't regret the distance, and I don't think the decision was wrong, but I'm human, and part of me grieves the relationship I longed for and didn't have.

Moving On Doesn't Mean Forgetting

What people usually mean when they tell you to move on, whether they realize it or not, is to stop feeling anything about it. But that's erasure, and it isn't possible because the relationship mattered.

Real closure is learning to live with the loss without letting it run your life. Grief therapist Gina Moffa calls this integration — instead of letting go of what you lost, you learn to carry it differently. You can experience both grief and gratitude simultaneously. You can miss someone and still know the distance was necessary. You can wish things had been different and still not want to go back. None of these are contradictions to resolve. They're just what it means to be human inside a complicated loss.

So how do you live alongside a loss like this? Here are four tips.

1. Name It as Grief. Many estranged people never let themselves acknowledge their grief because no one died. But this is a real loss and, in some ways, a harder one. Give it the same seriousness you'd give a friend grieving a death.

2. Make Peace With Not Knowing. It’s natural to try to force an ending; to slam the door shut for good or to rush back before you're ready. Both are usually attempts to escape the discomfort of not knowing how the story ends. Learning to say I don't know what will happen, and I can live with that, is one of the most freeing things you can do.

3. Build Your Own Rituals. Part of what makes this loss so heavy is that it comes with no ceremony to mark it. So, make one. Write the letter you'll never send. Do something gentle and deliberate on the painful anniversaries instead of gritting your teeth through them. It won't erase grief, but it gives it somewhere to go.

4. Measure Healing Differently. Don't measure your healing by how often the grief shows up. Measure it by what happens when it does. Does it take over for days, or does it pass more quickly than it used to? Can you feel it and still get on with your life? When the difficult moments pass faster and hit less often, that's healing, even if they never stop completely.

You Don't Have to “Get Over It”

Wherever you are on your journey, you don't have to be over it. You don't owe anyone a performance of being fine. What you're carrying is real, and the fact that you're still carrying it isn't a failure.

Maybe the useful question to ask yourself isn't "Why can't I get over this?" but What would it mean to stop trying to get over it and start learning to live beyond it?

item.title: Waiting Mode, Anxiety, and the Intolerance of Uncertainty
item.description:
Anxiety

Waiting Mode, Anxiety, and the Intolerance of Uncertainty

Why you can't focus or function when something is pending, ADHD or not.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Waiting mode is the inability to function or focus because something uncertain is pending.
  • The pattern is common in ADHD but may also be a trauma response in disguise.
  • Perfectionism and how safe you feel in the world may be at the root of the freeze.
  • The shift begins when you believe you can survive what comes without needing absolute control.

Waiting mode describes the inner experience of being unable to do anything because something uncertain, or a future event, is pending. It could be an appointment, an exam result, a medical scan, a conversation that has not happened yet, or a text message that may or may not receive a reply. The pending thing may be hours away or weeks away, significant or routine, but when you are in a waiting mode, that is what takes over your life, your attention, your energy, and your ability to focus. If you have an appointment at four in the afternoon, for the entire morning, you cannot do anything else. If you have an exam on Friday, the whole week is practically gone, and you live in suspension until then.

Although rationally you know there is nothing you need to do right now, mentally and emotionally, the unresolved thing clouds everything else. Life feels like it is in suspension. You are going through your day-to-day life, but not quite in it. You cannot relax, or rest, or work, or settle, because something does not feel right, or OK. Even if you resent feeling the way you feel, you cannot stop it.

Beyond ADHD Waiting Mode

Although not officially included in the DSM, the term waiting mode has, in recent years, gained traction in neurodivergent communities, more specifically with ADHD. For someone with ADHD, the waiting mode, although by and large unproductive in its overall outcome, serves a well-intentioned function. When a person's internal sense of time is unreliable, when they have a long history of missing appointments or underestimating how long things take, the waiting mode compensates for differences in executive function. The idea is that by suspending all activities and focusing only on what is pending, the brain will not miss it.

But waiting mode is not something that happens only with ADHD. The sense of keeping life in suspension whenever there is any pending uncertainty is also deeply familiar to people who have anxiety, particularly those with idealistic and perfectionistic tendencies, and among the emotionally intense and highly conscientious among us.

For those who have a tendency to hyperfixate on a future event and keep themselves in a waiting mode, the freeze is not a management device aimed at keeping track of time. There is something compulsive and obsessive in its quality. The mind locks onto the pending thing the way an intrusive thought locks into place: It is persistent, repetitive, and resistant to voluntary redirection. You may know rationally that your preoccupation is disproportionate. And yet you cannot just stop it with willpower, because the fixation is acting at a level deeper than conscious choice, one that involves your entire nervous system.

Uncertainty Intolerance and the Waiting Mode

Intolerance of uncertainty is a well-documented transdiagnostic factor that cuts across a myriad of depressive and anxiety disorders. People who are highly intolerant of uncertainty interpret ambiguous situations more negatively, show stronger physiological arousal when outcomes are unknown, and find it harder to function when they cannot predict or control what will happen next.

The waiting mode and its hyperfixation pattern are likely linked to perfectionistic and idealistic tendencies. Many of the people the term describes might never call themselves perfectionists because when they look at their lives, they mostly see how far things are from perfect. But perfectionism, at its root, is not about achieving real-life "perfection." It is a deep, often unconscious yearning for wholeness, for things to be complete, settled, and in their right place so the person can feel safe.

A Trauma Response in Disguise

We may also think of waiting mode as a form of a post-traumatic threat response, one that can follow from both complex developmental trauma (C-PTSD) and single-event trauma. In waiting mode, the body has essentially gone into a fight, flight, or fawn state. The mind has identified the pending uncertainty as the one missing piece that will restore safety. Every cognitive and emotional resource gets allocated to monitoring the perceived threat.

The origins of this pattern may reach far back into our early history. A child who grew up in a chaotic or unpredictable household, where warmth could be withdrawn without warning and safety was never guaranteed, learns early that the world is only safe when everything is under control. A child who was parentified, or a young person who was disadvantaged, bullied, or made to feel that they did not belong, learns that constant self-improvement and relentless optimisation are the only reliable routes to acceptance. The traumatised person learned, as a survival mechanism, to scan for anything that falls outside the smooth and expected pattern, and to treat that deviation as a signal of danger. The trouble is that the mechanism is no longer needed at the same intensity, but it has never been recalibrated. The hypervigilance now treats every open loop, every unresolved situation, as though it were as dangerous and as threatening as early childhood.

Another dimension of this pattern is where we place our locus of control when it comes to our sense of safety. For the person prone to waiting mode, it is as though their sense of safety lies not in their own resilience but in other people's appraisal, others' availability, others' love and attention. When those are going fine, they can breathe. When the signals shift or become uncertain, they feel paralysed.

Getting Out of Waiting Mode

If you slow down enough to listen to what is actually being believed in the moment of freezing, you may begin to hear the unconscious beliefs that have been quietly running your life. Things like: I need someone's approval to be safe. Or: I need to know the outcome before I am allowed to get on with my day. Or: If people know I screw up, that would be unbearable. These are not thoughts you have consciously chosen, but they have been operating in the background for so long that they no longer feel like beliefs you have adopted, but just the way things are.

But ultimately, to free yourself from constant loops of waiting mode may require deeper work than cognitive reframing or practical tips can offer. It is about how safe you feel in the world.

The waiting mode loosens its grip when something shifts in your relationship to life's uncertainty and imperfections. The hyperfixation is held in place by a conviction that you cannot afford for things to go wrong, that a bad outcome would not be survivable. The deeper shift is the growing, grudging, hard-won recognition that things can go wrong and you will be OK, that OK and survivable might be good enough, and that not everything needs to be optimised or maximised. The consequences, whatever they turn out to be, will come whether or not you welcome them, and you will deal with them when they do, just as you have many times before. You do not need the world to be settled before you are allowed to live your life. You don't need to be in full control to start living.

Perhaps you have always been more able to live on shaky ground than you give yourself credit for.

item.title: 3 Ways for Women Over 50 to Be Successful With Online Dating
item.description:
Mating

3 Ways for Women Over 50 to Be Successful With Online Dating

For older women in the dating pool, prioritising compatibility is key.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • Older women will be best off prioritising compatibility while dating, rather than "Consensual Mate Value."
  • With online dating, it helps to get specifics into your profile to resonate with the right person.
  • De-prioritise choosing men with the highest Consensual Mate Value.
  • Get off the app and meet up in person as soon as possible.
Source: Ivan S / Pexels

In my previous post, I explained the two types of “Mate Value” that affect attraction.

There’s “Consensual Mate Value” — or the immediate attractiveness a person has when you don’t know them, and then there’s “Unique Mate Value,” aka compatibility, that becomes more important in someone’s attractiveness assessment of you as they get to know you, or you them.

I pointed out that for older women in particular, it makes sense to meet potential partners in contexts that prioritise the compatibility element of mate value.

The obvious way to do this is to meet people in places where you can get to know them over time, like in clubs, classes, activities, or a workplace where you meet regularly. This means you can get to know each other’s idiosyncrasies and potentially increase attraction to, and desire for, each other — if there is compatibility between you.

It is worth noting that research by Kevin Kniffin & David Sloan Wilson of SUNY at Binghamton has demonstrated that when we get to know and like someone for their non-physical traits, e.g., personality or intelligence, we rate their physical attractiveness more highly.

The downside of this way of meeting potential partners — getting to know them over time — is that it is, by definition, very time-consuming.

It means committing yourself to attending the relevant events and spending time with multiple people to decide who you like, who you get on with, and who is actually available for a relationship.

As a dating consultant, then, I always recommend that my clients sign up for online dating as part of their mate search strategy, because it’s an efficient way of coming into contact with a large number of potential dating candidates. In fact, most of my clients find their partners via dating apps.

But I’m guessing it won’t have escaped your notice that it’s not easy to assess compatibility on a dating app. In fact, online dating encourages users to objectify each other, often to spend just a few seconds focusing on physical appearance in photos and maybe a few words in a bio before deciding to swipe left or right.

So, how are older women seeking a male, long-term partner, supposed to demonstrate high “Unique Mate Value” for the right person online?

3 things you can do to increase online dating satisfaction

1. Get specific in your profile/bio/prompt answers to resonate with the right man.

First, you’ll need to pick an app that allows a decent word count so you have a chance to tell the person reading your bio what makes you tick. This will generally mean going for one of the more traditional dating sites with longish onboarding processes rather than the “swipeable” apps, although if you can make good use of your prompt answers, the latter may still work well.

Then get specific in your profile or bio. Paint a picture of what your life is like, show off your quirks, tell a story of something that really floats your boat and how it made you feel. This will put off plenty of people, but it’ll resonate with, and help you stand out for, men you’re likely to be compatible with.

And of course, you’ll be able to assess men on whether or not they pick up on the specifics in your profile when messaging you, or whether they just send out copied and pasted messages that took little investment.

2. De-prioritise going for the highest “Consensual Mate Value" in men.

You might be tempted to go for the best-looking guys online, or those who seem to have high status or a great salary. To be fair, you don’t often have a lot more to go on in making your choice. But the problem is, these men will have high Consensual Mate Value, there will be lots of competition for their attention (and they know it), and so you’re far less likely to be able to have a relationship with such a man where they’ll value you in the way you’d like. High CMV does not equate to high value as a partner.

There’s even experimental evidence that good-looking men are not so nice, on average. According to a study by Michael Price and his colleagues at Brunel University in London, physically attractive men are less likely to be egalitarian and generous in the “dictator game” — a standard experimental economic task. The same effect has been found for wealthy men. The researchers speculate that such men have less to gain from being egalitarian because they possess higher social bargaining power. Attractive men don’t have to try so hard, so there’s less incentive to be nice.

When choosing a potential date, it may be better to focus on traits that suggest potential as a good, long-term partner: kindness, reliability, emotional stability, and, of course, compatibility.

While you might be able to get some clues about these traits from a well-written profile, you’ll generally be able to pin these down only once you start meeting in person, and this brings me on to the last point.

3. Get off the app and meet up as quickly as possible.

Don’t message with someone for ages. You’ll only be able to get a proper sense of what a man is like by getting face-to-face, at least on a video call. So once you’ve had four or five texts each way, I’d suggest it’s time to suggest a call, and if that goes well and you have a connection, the next step, of course, is to meet for an in-person date.

“Online” dating is something of a misnomer. The dating doesn’t happen online; it’s simply a forum to find potential dates to choose from. The crucial stuff happens when you get together — in real life — to assess that all-important compatibility.

item.title: The Nostalgic Self
item.description:
Nostalgia

The Nostalgic Self

Nostalgia offers us a way to reconnect with our disconnected self.

Posted July 9, 2026

Key points
  • "Self-discontinuity" is the feeling that our past self has become disconnected from our present self.
  • When we experience self-discontinuity, it is really our "self-concept" with which we have lost touch.
  • Studies show that nostalgic memories make people "feel more like their real self."
  • Nostalgia alleviates self-discontinuity by reconnecting us with our authentic self-concept.
Source: Klimkin / Pixabay

In a climactic scene from Disney’s The Lion King, the spirit of Mufasa appears to his son Simba in the clouds overhead and tells him, “You are more than what you have become.” In addition to spurring Simba on to challenge his uncle Scar and take his rightful place as king, this passage resonates personally, and perhaps a bit uncomfortably, with many viewers of the movie. As we make our way into, and through, adulthood, most of us at some point experience a moment where we feel that, like Simba, we are more than what we have become.

And for us, as for Simba, the reason for our failure to realize our full potential often lies in a basic act of forgetfulness. Mufasa tells Simba, “You have forgotten who you are,” and the same can be said of most of us when we look in the mirror one day and find that the demands and stresses of our life as we’re actually living it have caused us to lose touch with the life that we once imagined we would live, and the person we thought we would become.

Self-discontinuity

Psychologists call it “self-discontinuity,” the feeling that our past self and present self have become disconnected. And while for most of us the self from which we have become disconnected does not involve royal succession, that does not make it any less painful and disorienting when we wake up one day and realize that we have lost touch with it.

When we talk about losing touch with our “self,” of course, it’s not TV- or movie-plot amnesia we’re referring to, but rather our “self-concept,” the comprehensive perception we each have of our own identity, character, and nature. It is essentially the answer we would give to the question, “Who am I?” To lose touch with our self-concept is basically to forget the answer to that question, as Simba does in The Lion King.

Fortunately, there is a powerful remedy for combating self-discontinuity when we realize we are experiencing it, and it is the same one that allows Simba to resume his true role as king. After confronting his son with his forgetfulness of self, Mufasa leaves him with the final, simple command, “Remember.” It is through memory that Simba reclaims his throne, and it is through memory that we can reclaim our own true self. But it is not just recalling the autobiographical facts of our lives that will put us back in touch with our self. It is remembering the experiences—both important and trivial—that were meaningful to us in some way, and the way those experiences made us feel when we lived them. In other words, nostalgia.

Nostalgia and our life story

In his book Past Forward: How Nostalgia Can Help You Live a More Meaningful Life, psychologist Clay Routledge describes nostalgic memories as “self-defining,” citing numerous studies in which people report feeling like “nostalgic memories capture what is central to their self-concept more than other types of autobiographical memories.” Remembering the afternoon you taught your little sister to ride a bike, or the Valentine’s Day dinner on the night you became engaged to your spouse, or a glorious sunrise shared with friends on a senior year camping trip does more than just put a smile on your face and give you a warm feeling inside. It puts you in touch with some essential characteristic of your self by reminding you of something that once gave your life meaning. Or, as Routledge describes it, nostalgia “helps us craft a life story or narrative we can use to figure out how we want to define the self-concept.”

If we take Routledge’s concept of a “life story or narrative” a step further, and think of ourselves as the authors of this story, nostalgia can serve as a guiding principle similar to what the Greek philosopher Aristotle describes in his literary treatise The Poetics. To write a coherent, meaningful story or play, Aristotle argues, an author must present events, not as they actually happen, or might actually happen, in real life, but as they must happen according to the “law of probability and necessity.” In other words, everything that happens in a story must be consistent with the overarching artistic vision with which the story was first conceived, regardless of whether or not it is consistent with factual reality.

Criticizing writers who lose track of the plot by getting bogged down in nonessential details, Aristotle argues that “probable impossibilities” are always preferable to “improbable possibilities.” It is never a valid defense from criticism for an author to claim that an event or detail is “true to life” (i.e., that it is technically “possible”) if it is not logically consistent with the central theme of the story (i.e., probable).

Transferring this literary analogy to the life story that we are continually weaving out of the myriad experiences our days, weeks, months, and years offer as raw material, our self-concept is the central theme of our story—the narrative’s essential meaning. Like the “law of probability and necessity” that determines what events are included in a story, and how they are presented, our self-concept should be the shaping principle for determining the aspects of our lives that we include as central episodes in the plot of our ongoing life story.

At certain periods of our lives, however, we can find ourselves so heavily bombarded by events and experiences that, like the unfortunate writer in Aristotle’s Poetics, we get hung up on the peripheral “improbable possibilities” of real life and lose sight of the central theme of our life story. Like Simba, we wake up one day to find that we are more than we have become because we have forgotten who we are.

Calling up nostalgic memories from the past reminds us of what is truly important and meaningful to us, reorienting us to the plot line that the vicissitudes of life have caused us to lose sight of. By reminding us of who we really are, our nostalgic self is, in many ways, our truest self.
